title: Rook and the Missing Whistle
markdown:
The sun burst through Rook’s small window and painted the stone in stripes. Today was the King’s Grand Tea. The Duke and Duchess of Puddlewick would be there. Baron von Twee, who was never late, would be there. Rook, castle page, sat up on his cot and let his mind tick the way a pocket watch ticks: polish, perfect, prepare.

He took the grand staircases two at a time. Boots clicked. Stern kings and slumbering queens in their frames did not quite nod, though the light made it look as if they might. His destination was Ember’s Teashop, tucked against the side gate, a riot of cinnamon, mint, and that peculiar sparkle only a phoenix the size of a fist can put into a room.

Ember was already zipping between teacups. Tiny feathers shimmered like a sunrise that had decided to stay small.

“Morning, Rook!” Her voice was a tinkling bell through the clatter. “The Earl Grey is steeped. The scones are puffed. But oh—” Her glow flickered, a candle in a draught. “The special something is gone.”

Rook stopped in the doorway. “Gone? Did a crumb escape the biscuit tin?”

“No. Much more important.” She flapped, a puff of warm air on his nose. “The tinkly bit. The one that makes the big whistle sound.”

He scratched his head. A tinkly bit for a big whistle was a puzzle. Porcelain dragons danced around the rims of cups. Biscuits sat in buttery stacks. Earl Grey steamed as if nothing in the world had ever gone missing. “Are you sure? Perhaps it rolled under the counter.”

Ember’s head bobbed. “Brass. It makes a tweet that is just perfect for our surprise.”

He remembered then. Last year the surprise had been miniature sugar horses. This year the whispers had spoken of something with a sound that would make everyone clap. “The King’s surprise. We have to find it.”

They peeked into the kitchens first: steam from enormous pots, tall white hats, a clang of pans that would have hidden a small brass anything. Rook scanned hands and countertops and found nothing tinkly. He took a burlap sack from a hook. “We’ll check outside. Picture it, Ember. Where did you last have it?”

She flapped toward the side gate, her glow pulsing harder than usual, a tiny hidden engine. “I was showing it the sunshine. It made my glow brighter. Much brighter.”

He noticed it then. She was extra bright today, almost a miniature sun. “That’s odd. Are you all right?”

They dashed into town. Cobblestones clattered. People bustled. Rook scanned the ground left and right and found not a single brass scrap worth a tweet.

“Up ahead!” Ember darted like a firefly toward a construction site. Men in dust-covered aprons dug with powerful spades. Dark tunnels gaped. A freshly painted sign said: London Underground — Opening Soon.

“The underground?” Rook asked. “Is it for moles?”

“For people. Under the city. They say it’s very fast. They use steam.”

Steam. Brass. Tinkly. Whistle. Big sound. The King’s surprise. The new railway. An idea clicked, bright and bold. “Ember. The tinkly bit. Is it a steam whistle?”

Her glow flashed, brighter than any sunrise he had watched from a page’s window. “Yes. A little brass steam whistle. To make the grandest announcement for the King.”

Near a pile of damp dirt he spotted a discarded piece of brass, a few inches long, a hole at one end. It looked exactly like a tiny important whistle. “That’s it. Why is it here? Did you drop it?”

A deep rumble came from one of the tunnels. A puffing, like a giant with a cold. Then a long piercing blast that made the ground tremble.

“That’s the sound.” He pointed. “They’re testing the trains. They must be using the whistle to signal the runs.” He looked at Ember, who was now a dizzying kaleidoscope of light. “You didn’t just have it. You borrowed it.”

A tiny puff of smoke escaped her beak. “It was so shiny. When the sun hit it, my glow sang. I wanted everyone to see. I wanted to be extra bright for the important day.”

Another blast, longer, more insistent.

“The first train is leaving. If that whistle is still with them, we will never get it back.”

He grabbed her. “Hold on.” He sprinted for the entrance, down steep damp steps. The air grew cooler and tasted of earth and coal. People milled on the platform, eager to be first. A steam engine hissed and puffed, brass fittings gleaming like polished gold.

“There!” Ember pointed a glowing wing. Tucked in a small gap near the boiler, their whistle glinted in the dim.

A conductor with his cap askew blew a much bigger whistle. The engine roared. Steam billowed. Rook had seconds. He did not hesitate. He leaped onto the footplate. As the engine lurched, he snatched the little brass thing, fingers fumbling but firm.

“Got it!” The din ate the word. The train picked up speed and chugged into the echoing dark. The whistle was warm and smooth in his hand. Ember on his shoulder glowed like a beacon that had decided not to flicker.

With a grunt and a slide he got himself off the footplate and landed on the platform as the train vanished. He clutched the whistle. “We got it.”

Back at the castle the guests were already a low hum in the Great Hall. Rook, Ember perched proud, dashed to the King’s table. He held up the brass. The King beamed. Ember, with a flourish, let out a tiny perfect tweet. Then the King took the whistle and blew.

The sound filled the hall and silenced the murmurs. All eyes turned to a hidden alcove. A troop of tiny clockwork automatons, powered by steam, marched out and trumpeted miniature trumpets. The guests erupted. Even Baron von Twee managed an enthusiastic clap.

Rook grinned until it reached his ears. A castle page and a teashop phoenix with a habit of borrowing shiny things had got the surprise to the table. Ember settled on his shoulder, glow ordinary again, which was still quite a lot of glow. The Earl Grey, when they finally sat, tasted exactly as steeped.
